curation.lead:
The Humpty Dumpty Institute (HDI) is a New York nonprofit incorporated on October 19, 1998 (NY Corp #2307873, EIN 13-4028567), originally registered at the Central Park West apartment of co-founder Michael W. Sonnenfeldt. Its stated mission — organizing Congressional Delegations (CODELs) and facilitating dialogue between U.S. lawmakers and foreign governments — provided a framework for what became one of the more unusual influence pipelines documented in the Jeffrey Epstein files. Mark Epstein, Jeffrey’s brother, served on the HDI board of directors, signed its 2015 IRS 990 return, loaned the organization over $100,000 in 2014, and personally participated in all-expenses-paid first-class delegations to Bahrain and Azerbaijan. When delegation slots opened up on a May 2014 trip to Baku, Mark forwarded the recruitment email directly to Jeffrey, offering him the ability to place people from “media, finance, banking, education” on a Congressional delegation that would meet Azerbaijan’s president.

HDI’s significance extends well beyond the Epstein connection. The organization has run 52 or more CODELs to over 30 countries, hosting 250+ Members of Congress and 400+ senior staffers. Its Congressional Advisory Board at one point included 33 current and former lawmakers spanning both parties, from Maxine Waters and Jim Clyburn to Mark Meadows and Adam Schiff. These relationships gave HDI substantial access to the U.S. legislative branch — access that became geopolitically consequential when HDI formalized a partnership with Beijing’s Taihe Institute in August 2017. Taihe employs 12 or more current and former CCP and PLA members as senior fellows. The partnership drew media scrutiny and Congressional resignations from the HDI advisory board, yet HDI maintained the relationship through at least the September 2019 Taihe Civilizations Forum in Beijing.

Structurally, HDI occupies a regulatory blind spot. Despite maintaining a partnership with a CCP-linked think tank while simultaneously operating the largest private CODEL pipeline in the United States, HDI has zero FARA registrations and zero lobbying filings in Senate LDA records. Comparable organizations facilitating China-U.S. influence activities — such as the China-United States Exchange Foundation — have registered under FARA with multiple registrants. HDI’s 990 filings also flag anomalies: the 2015 return declared “Yes” on both excess benefit transactions with a disqualified person and participation in prohibited tax shelter transactions, and disclosed foreign bank accounts. Meanwhile, HDI’s revenue collapsed over 80% from a peak of $1.82 million in 2011 to under $200,000 by 2018, a pattern of financial contraction that mirrors — at smaller scale — the decline seen at IPI. A partial recovery to $221,000 by 2023 may reflect new funding sources entirely unrelated to the Epstein orbit.

What explains the 2015 990 flags for excess benefit transactions and prohibited tax shelter participation? Who was the disqualified person, and what was the nature of the tax shelter?

Who funded HDI during its revenue collapse from $1.82M (2011) to under $200K (2018)? Were there foreign government contributions routed through intermediaries that would not appear on U.S. nonprofit filings?
What is the relationship between HDI and IPI beyond the connection documented in the database? Did they share donors, board members, or coordinate CODEL activities?

Has the DOJ National Security Division or any Congressional committee examined HDI’s Taihe partnership for potential FARA violations? If not, why not, given the documented CCP/PLA connections and Congressional access?
What role did Robert Lawrence Kuhn — another figure operating at the intersection of U.S.-China influence and Epstein-adjacent networks — play in relation to HDI or Taihe?

The most structurally significant relationship is with Jeffrey Epstein, mediated through his brother Mark Epstein. Mark served as an HDI director, signed the 2015 IRS 990 return as “Mark L. Epstein, Director,” loaned the organization over $100,000 in 2014, and participated in CODELs to Bahrain (2013) and Azerbaijan (2014). In a December 22, 2014 email (EFTA02598877), Mark wrote to Jeffrey: “We (Humpty Dumpty Institute) led a congressional delegation to Bahrain to meet with ministers and the president (king/head poobah), opposition leaders, senate, head of the US Navy 5th fleet (headquartered in Bahrain) etc.” He added: “I did not know you were doing this kind of stuff. I was also on one to Azerbaijan, and might go on one to Turkey/Cypress in March.” The casual tone suggests this was an ongoing communication channel about HDI activities that Jeffrey was already aware of through other means.

Amir Dossal, former United Nations Chief of Partnerships and chairman of the Global Partnership Forum, served as an ex officio director of HDI. Dossal provides the UN institutional bridge: on June 20, 2013, he co-hosted a UN event on oceans and Sustainable Development Goals alongside Ghislaine Maxwell (representing the TerraMar Project) and Stuart Beck, Palau’s ambassador. This event placed an HDI director in direct programmatic collaboration with Maxwell at the United Nations. In August 2011, Dossal appeared alongside Deutsche Bank Global Head of Asset Management Kevin Parker and Russian Duma member Ilya Ponomarev at the New York Academy of Sciences “Science & the City Gala,” which honored UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon and featured James Simons, James Watson, and Jack Rosen — figures who surface repeatedly across the broader Epstein network.

The HDI board as revealed by the 2015 990 filing was a 14-member body chaired by Dr. Al Khalafalla, with chairman emeriti Constance Milstein (later a Biden ambassador nominee to Malta) and Sonnenfeldt. Other directors included William J. Rouhana Jr. (co-founder and chairman since 2010, CEO of Chicken Soup for the Soul Entertainment), former Congressman Benjamin Gilman, Walter Arbib (SkyLink Group president), and Jay T. Snyder (HBJ Investments). The co-founder and president since 1998, Ralph L. Cwerman, drew $145,458 in annual compensation. Executive Director Joseph Merante, a former State Department Foreign Service officer, managed the CODEL pipeline and served as the operational point of contact for delegation logistics and the Taihe partnership.

sections.title: The Congressional Delegation Pipeline
sections.content:
HDI’s core operational activity — and its primary source of political influence — is the organization of private Congressional Delegations. Over the past two decades, HDI has organized 52 or more CODELs to over 30 countries, hosting more than 250 Members of Congress and 400 senior Congressional staff members. Destinations have included Azerbaijan, Bahrain, Turkey, Cyprus, and UN headquarters in New York. The delegations are fully funded and “entirely first class with all first class accommodations,” according to CODEL recruitment emails found in Epstein’s files (EFTA02718091).

The mechanics of this pipeline are documented in unusual detail thanks to the May 2014 Azerbaijan delegation. When participants dropped out of the trip, HDI Executive Director Joseph Merante emailed seeking replacements from “media, finance, banking, education.” Mark Epstein forwarded Merante’s email directly to Jeffrey Epstein on May 22, 2014, writing: “In case you know someone and want to do them a favor: (let me know).” The full agenda, recovered from Epstein’s document files (EFTA02725237), reveals meetings with President Ilham Aliyev, U.S. Ambassador Richard Morningstar, Foreign Affairs Minister Elmar Mammadyarov, and parliamentary committees. This was a delegation that provided face-to-face access to a head of state — and Jeffrey Epstein had the ability to fill empty seats.

The Congressional Advisory Board, as constituted around 2022, included 33 or more current and former members of Congress from both parties: Don Bacon (R-NE), Andre Carson (D-IN), Judy Chu (D-CA), Jim Clyburn (D-SC), Ruben Gallego (D-AZ), Andy Harris (R-MD), Jim Himes (D-CT), Gregory Meeks (D-NY), Bennie Thompson (D-MS), Maxine Waters (D-CA), Debbie Wasserman Schultz (D-FL), and others. Former advisory board members include Mark Meadows, Adam Schiff, and Sheila Jackson Lee. The breadth of this bipartisan Congressional roster is itself a form of institutional credibility — one that made the later Taihe Institute partnership possible.

sections.title: The Taihe Institute Partnership and CCP Nexus
sections.content:
In August 2017, HDI formalized a partnership with the Beijing-based Taihe Institute, a think tank whose senior fellows include 12 or more current and former members of the Chinese Communist Party and the People’s Liberation Army. HDI Executive Director Merante participated in the Taihe Civilizations Forum in Beijing in both August 2017 and September 2019. Ruby Wang, Senior Vice President at Perfect World (a Chinese gaming company) and a Taihe fellow, joined the HDI board, serving as a bridge figure between the two organizations.

The partnership drew significant scrutiny. The Washington Examiner reported on HDI’s CCP connections, and multiple members of Congress resigned from the Advisory Board. Taihe co-authored a report with HDI-adjacent figures that called the United States a “failed country” and promoted the conspiracy theory that COVID-19 leaked from a Maryland military base. HDI’s public response was to state that it “never accepted any funds from the Taihe Institute or any Chinese Government organ or entity.” Whether this denial addresses the full scope of the relationship is an open question: FARA’s definition of “agent of a foreign principal” under 22 USC 611(c) does not require direct funding — acting “at the order, request, or under the direction or control” of a foreign principal is sufficient.

The combination is what makes HDI structurally anomalous: a single organization simultaneously operating the largest private CODEL pipeline in the country, maintaining a formal partnership with a CCP/PLA-linked think tank, seating an Epstein family member on its board, and doing so with zero FARA registrations and zero LDA lobbying filings. Comparable China-U.S. influence organizations — specifically the China-United States Exchange Foundation — have registered under FARA with four separate registrants (Capitol Counsel #6328, Wilson Global #6584, BLJ Worldwide #5875, BGR Government Affairs #5430). HDI’s functional equivalent activities remain entirely unregistered.

sections.title: Financial Profile and Contraction
sections.content:
HDI’s IRS 990 filings trace a steep financial decline. Revenue peaked at $1.82 million in 2011, sustained at $1.64 million (2012) and $1.70 million (2013), then began accelerating downward: $1.47 million (2015), $481,000 (2016), $401,000 (2017), $227,000 (2018). A brief spike to $360,000 in 2019 was followed by continued attrition: $202,000 (2020), $155,000 (2021), $174,000 (2022), and $221,000 (2023). Total assets peaked at $287,000 in 2011 and remained minimal at $170,000 in 2023. This represents over 80% revenue decline — far exceeding normal nonprofit fluctuation.

The financial picture contains several flags. Mark Epstein loaned HDI over $100,000 in 2014, per the 990 filing — a personal loan from a board director that raises governance questions about the organization’s independence. The 2015 return, signed by Mark Epstein as director, flagged “Yes” on Line 25a (excess benefit transaction with a disqualified person) and Line 5a (party to a prohibited tax shelter transaction), and disclosed foreign bank accounts. These are IRS red flags that rarely appear on legitimate nonprofit filings, individually or in combination.

The revenue decline parallels — at much smaller scale — the pattern observed at IPI, whose assets fell 73% from $12.6 million to $3.9 million over a similar period. Both organizations are connected to the Epstein network through different pathways (HDI through Mark Epstein and Dossal; IPI through Terje Rod-Larsen and Gratitude America). The partial revenue recovery in 2022–2023 may signal new funding sources entirely unrelated to the Epstein orbit, but without granular donor data from the 990s, the source of the recovery cannot be determined.

sections.title: Regulatory Gaps and Disclosure Failures
sections.content:
HDI exists in a regulatory vacuum that appears to be structural rather than accidental. The organization has zero FARA registrations despite its partnership with the CCP-linked Taihe Institute and its role facilitating meetings between U.S. lawmakers and foreign heads of state including Azerbaijan’s President Aliyev. It has zero lobbying filings in Senate LDA records despite maintaining a 33-member Congressional Advisory Board and organizing 52 or more CODELs. This absence of disclosure is not merely a technicality — it means that an organization with documented CCP institutional ties and documented Epstein family involvement in its governance has operated one of the most significant Congressional access pipelines in the country entirely outside federal transparency requirements.

The FARA question is particularly pointed. Under 22 USC 611(c), the definition of “agent of a foreign principal” encompasses anyone who acts “at the order, request, or under the direction or control” of a foreign principal, or who “acts in any other capacity at the order, request, or under the direction or control, of a foreign principal.” HDI’s Taihe partnership involved joint events, shared speakers, and co-produced publications — activities that, when performed by other organizations with Chinese government connections, have triggered FARA registration requirements. HDI’s defense — that it received no funds from Taihe or any Chinese government entity — addresses only the funding prong and does not resolve whether the partnership constitutes direction, control, or agent-of status under the broader statutory framework.

The 990 filing anomalies compound the picture. An organization that flags excess benefit transactions, prohibited tax shelter participation, and foreign bank accounts while its primary board-level relationship is with the brother of a convicted sex offender who was channeling delegation recruitment through that very board member — this combination of regulatory gaps would warrant examination in any systematic review of nonprofit compliance. That no such review has occurred is itself an open question for investigators.
